format: Each lesson has five formative questions (error, guided1, guided2, independent1, independent2) then two distinct required-check questions. Each row is prompt, correct option, distractors, explanatory feedback.

10: A learner calls an antibody the antigen on a microbe. What is the correction?
An antigen is a recognized feature; an antibody is a protein that may bind a matching feature.
Both words mean the same immune cell.
Antigens are always antibiotics.
The two molecules have different roles in recognition and binding.
In the workbook's simplified five-step sequence, which event starts the model?
A pathogen enters and early cells encounter it.
Memory cells appear before any target exists.
An antibody is made by a red blood cell.
The model begins with encounter and early response before specific activation.
Which is an example of passive immunity?
Receiving antibodies made by another source.
Building one's own response after vaccination.
Rebuilding a physical barrier rather than making a targeted immune response.
Passive protection supplies antibodies rather than forming the same active response.
Why is the CBE chart's 'active immunity is permanent' claim too broad?
Protection and memory can vary by agent, vaccine and time.
Immune responses never form memory.
Only passive antibodies exist.
Active responses can persist but do not guarantee lifelong complete protection.
A learner says antibodies alone directly destroy every pathogen. What is missing?
Antibody binding can block or mark targets, while other cells and mechanisms may be needed.
Antibodies are bacteria that divide independently.
An antibody is a population-level warning rather than a protein in an immune response.
The immune response is a coordinated network, not one universal killing step.
Which branch belongs under acquired immunity in the workbook flowchart?
Active response by the person and passive receipt of antibodies.
Only intact skin and cilia.
Only public sanitation, with no targeted response within the body.
Adaptive/acquired protection can arise through the person's response or supplied antibodies.
What makes the five-step diagram a useful but limited model?
It identifies roles and an approximate sequence, while actual immune events overlap and vary.
Every antigen follows one exact clock sequence.
Its numbered arrows prove all infections have the same outcome.
A model simplifies complex interacting processes and needs its scope stated.
11: A learner says O-negative blood can always be given to anyone without tests. What is wrong?
The shorthand concerns red-cell compatibility; clinical selection and testing still matter.
O-negative means all blood products are identical.
The ABO system has no antigens.
A broad emergency red-cell donor type is not a universal no-test rule.
What makes an A-to-B red-cell mismatch hazardous in the classroom model?
A recipient's antibodies may react with incompatible donor red-cell antigens.
Family relationship matters more than antigen matching for red-cell compatibility.
A respiratory virus is the key factor in ABO red-cell matching.
The model links red-cell antigens with the recipient's antibody response.
Which statement describes modern vaccine platforms accurately?
Different vaccines may use attenuated organisms, inactivated material, components or mRNA approaches.
Every vaccine is a dead whole pathogen.
Every vaccine gives passive maternal antibodies.
The Canadian Immunization Guide describes more than the older two-category shorthand.
A prepared antibody product and a vaccine are compared. Which difference matters?
The product supplies antibodies; vaccination stimulates the recipient's own active response.
Both always last forever.
Both are red-cell transfusions.
The source of antibodies and potential immune memory differ.
How should the CBE vaccine/autism page be handled?
Exclude its false debate framing; the Canadian Immunization Guide states MMR does not cause autism.
Teach both claims as equally supported scientific positions.
Omit all vaccine science because the old page is wrong.
A dated source claim needs correction, not false balance.
Which claim about blood products is carefully qualified?
O-negative red cells often have a broad emergency role, while plasma and patient testing follow their own rules.
O-negative plasma and red cells are universally interchangeable.
ABO typing alone predicts every transfusion reaction.
Compatibility is component-specific and clinically assessed.
A student says vaccination guarantees lifelong protection from every infection. What is the correction?
Protection depends on the target, vaccine, schedule, response and time; no universal guarantee follows.
Vaccines never stimulate memory.
Only antibiotics can prevent infection.
Vaccination can build protection without making every outcome absolute.
12: A learner says antibiotics make a person's body resistant so they no longer work. What is the error?
Resistance refers to bacteria able to survive a medicine, not the body becoming immune to it.
Viruses are bacterial cells.
A medicine that reduces symptoms also kills the organism causing them.
Selection can increase resistant bacteria; the host's body is not the resistant organism.
Why does an antibiotic not directly treat a typical viral cold?
Its bacterial targets are not the cold virus's replication machinery.
A viral infection always contains no symptoms.
The dose is always too small for any illness.
Mechanism depends on the type of infectious agent.
Two non-prescription products list the same active ingredient. What is the first safety concern?
Combining them may duplicate the ingredient and exceed directions.
Different brand names guarantee the active ingredients cannot overlap.
Every combination is automatically safer.
Ingredient lines and dose directions matter more than brand names.
A friend offers leftover antibiotics for a new illness. Which response matches current guidance?
Do not share them; seek appropriate professional assessment and use medicines as directed.
Use them because any infection is bacterial.
Change the label instructions to fit the leftovers.
Antibiotics need an appropriate indication and directed use.
Why can unnecessary antibiotic use contribute to resistance?
It can select bacteria with traits that survive the drug and multiply.
It trains the immune response by causing the body to produce an infection indefinitely.
It sterilizes all environments permanently.
Selection changes the composition of bacterial populations over time.
Which statement distinguishes antibiotic, antiviral and symptom-relief purposes?
They target different problems; a symptom product may ease discomfort without removing the virus.
All three are identical cures for every infection.
An antibiotic is a vaccine for viral colds.
Match a product to its mechanism and purpose, not just the word 'medicine'.
What should a learner do when label warnings or interactions are unclear?
Read the active ingredients and directions and ask a pharmacist or clinician for individual advice.
Guess a dose from a class example.
Ignore the warning if the product is sold without a prescription.
Classroom label literacy cannot replace personal medical guidance.
09: A learner says redness after a sliver proves a particular bacterium is present. What is the error?
Inflammation can follow sterile injury; symptoms alone do not identify an organism.
Inflammation can only occur after vaccination.
Redness alone identifies a specific inherited disorder.
Redness, warmth and swelling show a response but are not organism-specific evidence.
Which structure helps move mucus and trapped particles along airways?
Cilia on airway cells.
A blood cell circulating nearby, without crossing the damaged barrier.
An antibody in the environment rather than a cell responding at the wound.
Cilia support clearance after mucus traps inhaled material.
What can a macrophage do in an early response?
Engulf microbes or debris and help coordinate further defence.
Become a red-cell antigen.
Inflammation immediately rebuilds the damaged skin barrier.
A macrophage is an immune cell that can engulf material; it is not an antibody molecule.
A student says a cough after smoke exposure proves infection. Which response is strongest?
Smoke can irritate airways and impair clearance; coughing alone does not diagnose infection.
Coughing always has one bacterial cause.
Smoke improves cilia movement in every case.
A symptom can arise through more than one mechanism.
Why might a sliver site be warm and swollen?
Local signals change blood flow and fluid movement while immune cells arrive.
Inflammation converts damaged body cells into invading microbes.
Only antibodies from a vaccine can cause warmth.
Inflammation involves tissue signals, blood vessels and immune-cell movement.
Which ordering fits a breached skin barrier?
Entry opportunity → tissue signals and inflammation → immune cells help clear material.
Antibody first → skin forms a sliver → no tissue response.
All pathogens disappear before a barrier is breached.
A breach creates the opportunity; the local response follows injury or entry.
The workbook barrier chart asks for structures and functions. What is a complete answer?
Match each named structure to how it blocks, traps or clears material and note its limits.
Write 'immune system' in every blank.
Assume every barrier is an antibody.
The source task is about distinct physical or chemical mechanisms at entry points.
